title: A Tour of the Standard Library

questions.prompt: Which two tiny interfaces underpin most I/O in Go?
questions.explanation: io.Reader (a Read method) and io.Writer (a Write method) are satisfied by files, buffers, and network connections, so I/O code composes.

questions.prompt: Which struct fields does `encoding/json` marshal and unmarshal?
questions.explanation: Reflection-based encoders can only see exported fields; unexported fields silently disappear. Use `json:"..."` tags for the JSON names.

questions.prompt: To build a string efficiently in a loop, use strings.____ instead of repeated +=.
questions.explanation: `strings.Builder` accumulates into one growing buffer, avoiding a new string allocation on every += concatenation.

questions.prompt: In a `time.Format` layout, what reference date do you write the layout as?
questions.explanation: Go's time layout is the specific reference time Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006; you write the layout by spelling that date/time out.

questions.prompt: Match the need to a good standard-library choice — which are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: strconv converts between strings and numbers
bufio.Scanner reads input a line at a time
os.ReadFile reads a whole file into a []byte
fmt is required to open network sockets

questions.explanation: strconv parses/formats numbers, bufio.Scanner scans lines, and os.ReadFile slurps a file. fmt formats and prints; it doesn't open sockets.

questions.prompt: Match each fmt verb to what it prints.

pairs.right: A struct with its field names

questions.explanation: %+v adds field names, %T shows the type, %q quotes strings, and %w wraps errors so they stay inspectable.
